A close reading for the week

“The cognomen of Crane was not inapplicable”

Sleepy Hollow · Ichabod Crane

Before the headless horseman and the pumpkin, Irving gives his schoolmaster a body, built joint by joint out of comic similes until the man is a scarecrow the reader can already see running.

The cognomen of Crane was not inapplicable to his person.1 He was tall, but exceedingly lank, with narrow shoulders, long arms and legs, hands that dangled a mile out of his sleeves, feet that might have served for shovels,2 and his whole frame most loosely hung together.

  1. 1

    A name that fits

    “Cognomen” is Latin for a surname, and the mock-learned word sets the tone: Irving’s narrator is a genial antiquarian, amused by his own vocabulary. “Not inapplicable” is a comic double negative: the name Crane fits perfectly, and the narrator says so as mildly as possible. The whole portrait will be delivered in this voice of polite understatement wrapped around ruthless caricature.

  2. 2

    Hands and feet

    His hands “dangled a mile out of his sleeves”, and his feet “might have served for shovels”. The hyperbole is American tall-tale, and the details are practical: sleeves too short, feet like tools. Ichabod is a Connecticut Yankee schoolmaster, poor and made of angles, and Irving assembles him from the extremities inward, as a caricaturist would draw him.
